title: True & False
objectives: Compare values and return TRUE or FALSE
Recognise how boundary values affect a comparison
about: A comparison checks whether two values meet a rule. Excel returns TRUE when the rule is met and FALSE when it is not. You can compare numbers, dates, text, or cell references. A manager might check whether stock is below its reorder point or whether a payment date has passed. Use comparison operators when you need a clear yes-or-no result, not a custom label. Start with an equals sign, select the first value, add the operator, then select the second value. The result updates whenever either value changes. The comparison is recalculated automatically when either value changes.
syntax:
=value1 operator value2
= equal to · > greater than · < less than
>= greater than or equal to · <= less than or equal to · <> not equal to

examples.scenario: A delivery manager checks a shipment target.
examples.why: 120 is greater than or equal to 100.

examples.scenario: A teacher checks a score below the pass mark.
An accounts clerk checks whether two status labels differ.
examples.why: The two text values are not equal.

watch_out: Use >= when the boundary itself should pass; > excludes it.
Text comparisons depend on the actual text values.
A comparison returns TRUE or FALSE, not a custom status label.
recap: Comparison operators test a rule and return TRUE or FALSE. Lesson 37 uses that result inside IF to display a useful label.

title: IF Function
objectives: Test one condition with IF
Return one result when TRUE and another when FALSE
Use text and numeric results in IF
about: IF lets a formula make a decision. It checks one condition and returns one result when the condition is TRUE, then another when it is FALSE. Use it to label orders, flag overdue invoices, assign pass or fail results, or show whether stock needs attention. The condition is usually a comparison such as B2>100 or A2="East". After the condition, enter the value for TRUE, then the value for FALSE. Text results need quotation marks, while numbers do not. Choose the comparison carefully: > excludes the boundary, while >= includes it. IF returns only one of its two results for each row.
syntax:
=IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false)
logical_test: the condition Excel checks
value_if_true: result when TRUE
value_if_false: result when FALSE

examples.scenario: A retailer labels a sale above 100.
A school records a pass at 50 or more.
A service team checks whether a ticket is closed.
examples.why: The text does not match Closed.

watch_out: Put text results inside double quotation marks.
The TRUE result comes before the FALSE result.
Check whether the rule uses > or >=; the boundary can change the outcome.
recap: IF tests one condition and returns one of two results. Lesson 38 adds multiple conditions with AND, OR and XOR.

title: AND, OR, XOR Functions
objectives: Require all conditions with AND
Accept any matching condition with OR
Test whether exactly one of two conditions is true with XOR
about: AND, OR and XOR combine logical tests into one TRUE or FALSE result. AND requires every test to pass. OR needs at least one test to pass. XOR is different: it returns TRUE when an odd number of tests are TRUE, so with two tests, exactly one must pass. Use these functions when a decision depends on several details, such as region and sales, payment and stock, or priority and waiting time. Put each test inside the function, separated by commas. You can use the result directly or place it inside IF to return a label. Write the rule in plain English first; that makes the choice between AND and OR clearer.

examples.scenario: A bonus requires East region and sales of at least 500.
A case is urgent when High priority or older than 24 hours.
A promotion applies when exactly one condition is met.
examples.why: Only the customer-type condition is TRUE.

watch_out: AND means all conditions; OR means at least one.
XOR is not the same as OR when multiple conditions are TRUE.
Text inside a test needs quotation marks.
recap: AND, OR and XOR combine tests. Lesson 39 uses IS functions to identify the kind of value a cell contains.

title: IS Functions
objectives: Test whether a cell is blank, numeric, text or logical
Use ISBLANK, ISNUMBER, ISTEXT and ISLOGICAL inside IF
Distinguish a real number from digits stored as text
about: IS functions check what kind of value a cell contains. They return TRUE or FALSE, which makes them useful inside IF when imported or incomplete data needs review. ISBLANK checks for an empty cell. ISNUMBER checks for a numeric value, while ISTEXT checks for text. ISLOGICAL checks for Excel TRUE and FALSE values. A date is stored as a number, so ISNUMBER returns TRUE for a valid Excel date. Digits stored as text are still text; ISNUMBER does not convert them. Use the test that matches the issue you need to catch, then let IF display a clear status. These checks identify data types, not whether an entry is sensible.

An accounts clerk checks an invoice amount.
A staff import contains digits stored as text.
examples.why: The entry is text even though it looks numeric.

watch_out: A formula returning an empty string is not a truly empty cell for ISBLANK.
ISNUMBER does not convert text-formatted numbers.
Excel stores dates as numbers, so ISNUMBER can return TRUE for dates.
recap: IS functions identify the type of value in a cell. Lesson 40 uses several conditions to assign one of many results.

title: IFS Function
objectives: Return a result for the first condition that is TRUE
Order conditions from most specific to broadest
Add a final TRUE condition as the fallback
about: IFS checks several conditions in order and returns the result linked to the first condition that is TRUE. It is useful for grading bands, stock labels, service priorities and commission rates. Each condition is followed by the value to return when that condition passes. Excel stops at the first match, so order matters. Put higher thresholds before lower ones when bands overlap. Add TRUE as the final condition to catch anything that did not match earlier tests. Without a catch-all, a value outside every listed band can return #N/A. IFS is available in Excel 2019 and later. In older versions, use nested IF functions.

examples.scenario: A school assigns letter grades from exam scores.
A warehouse labels stock by urgency.
A service desk assigns priority from waiting time.
examples.why: Thirty hours passes the second condition.

watch_out: Check conditions in the correct order; IFS returns the first match.
Include a final TRUE condition to avoid #N/A for unmatched values.
Needs Excel 2019 or later. In older versions, use nested IF functions.
recap: IFS handles several outcomes in one formula. Lesson 41 uses SWITCH when one expression is matched against exact values.

title: SWITCH Function
objectives: Match one expression against several exact values
Return a result for each matching value
Set a default result for unmatched values
about: SWITCH compares one expression with a list of exact values and returns the result paired with the first match. It is useful when a code or status has several possible labels, such as route directions, shift names, payment states or ticket priorities. Enter the expression first, then each value and its result as a pair. Add a final default result for values that do not match any pair. SWITCH is easier to read than a long chain of IF functions when one cell is compared with fixed options. It does not test ranges such as greater than 100; use IF or IFS for thresholds. SWITCH is available in Excel 2019 and later.

examples.why: N matches the first value-result pair.

A payment report handles an unlisted code.
examples.why: No listed code matches, so the default is returned.

watch_out: SWITCH checks exact matches, not ranges such as >=500.
Keep text match values in quotation marks; numeric values do not need them.
Needs Excel 2019 or later. In older versions, use nested IF functions.
recap: SWITCH maps one exact value to one result. Lesson 42 combines IF with other functions for more involved decisions.

title: IF Combinations
objectives: Combine IF with AND or OR
Use nested IF when a decision has more than two outcomes
Order overlapping conditions from most specific to broadest
about: You can combine IF with other functions when a decision depends on several rules or has more than two possible outcomes. Use AND inside IF when every condition must pass, and OR when any one condition is enough. A nested IF places another IF inside the first formula result, letting you check a second rule when the first one fails. This is useful for grading bands, stock alerts and approval levels. Write each rule in plain English before building the formula. Put the most specific condition first when thresholds overlap. Check the order of the true and false results, and use parentheses to keep each decision together.

A help desk marks a ticket urgent for High priority or a long wait.
examples.why: The priority test alone is enough.

examples.why: The first and second tests both fail.

watch_out: AND requires every condition; OR requires at least one.
In nested IF, a false result can contain another IF.
Put the most specific threshold first when conditions overlap.
recap: Combined IF formulas handle multi-condition rules and several outcomes. The checkpoint brings together comparisons, AND and IFS.
